claim: Proteasomal protein degradation is a key determinant of protein half-life.
source: Proteasomal protein degradation is a key determinant of protein half-life and hence of cellular processes ranging from basic metabolism to a host of immunological processes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: The mechanisms regulating proteasome activity are only incompletely understood.
source: Despite its importance the mechanisms regulating proteasome activity are only incompletely understood.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as motivation for the study.

claim: The 20S proteasome is a dynamic enzyme and its activity varies over time.
source: The 20S proteasome is a dynamic enzyme and its activity varies over time because of interactions between substrates and products and the proteolytic and regulatory sites
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The locations of proteolytic and regulatory sites and the interactions between them are predicted by the model and experimentally supported.
source: the locations of these sites and the interactions between them are predicted by the model, and experimentally supported.
evidence: This claim is supported by both modeling predictions and experimental validation as stated in the abstract.

claim: The rate-limiting step of hydrolysis is the transport of the substrates into the proteasome.
source: The analysis suggests that the rate-limiting step of hydrolysis is the transport of the substrates into the proteasome.
evidence: This is a major finding stated in the abstract and supported by modeling and experimental data.

claim: The transport efficiency varies between human standard- and immuno-proteasomes.
source: The transport efficiency varies between human standard- and immuno-proteasomes thereby impinging upon total degradation rate and substrate cleavage-site usage.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by comparative analysis.

claim: Proteasomes are at the core of the ubiquitin-proteasome system and responsible for the destruction of the majority of the cytoplasmic proteins.
source: Here we apply a modelling approach to a detailed mechanistic analysis of proteasomes, which are at the core of the ubiquitin-proteasome system and responsible for the destruction of the majority of the cytoplasmic proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: Proteins are usually tagged by E1-E2-E3-E4 enzyme-mediated poly-ubiquitination before being carried into the proteasome proteolytic chamber.
source: Proteins are usually tagged by E1-E2-E3-E4 enzyme-mediated poly-ubiquitination, carried into the proteasome proteolytic chamber where they are fragmented and, ultimately, expulsed (Schwartz and Ciechanover, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Oxidised proteins can be degraded by 20S proteasomes without prior poly-ubiquitination.
source: Proteins, and especially oxidised proteins—that is, those that reflect the presence of cellular stress conditions—can also be degraded by 20S proteasomes without prior poly-ubiquitination (Aiken et al., 2011; Pickering and Davies, 2012; Ben-Nissan and Sharon, 2014; Höhn and Grune, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: 20S proteasomes are present in cells.
source: In addition to stress response, the 20S proteasomes present in cells (Fabre et al., 2015) have been shown to regulate the abundance of a host of signalling molecules involved in cell cycle progression, cellular growth control and oncogenesis (Ben-Nissan and Sharon, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: 20S proteasomes regulate the abundance of signalling molecules involved in cell cycle progression, cellular growth control and oncogenesis.
source: the 20S proteasomes present in cells (Fabre et al., 2015) have been shown to regulate the abundance of a host of signalling molecules involved in cell cycle progression, cellular growth control and oncogenesis (Ben-Nissan and Sharon, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: 20S proteasomes form the core of the structure of 26S proteasomes.
source: Additionally, 20S proteasomes form the core of the structure of 26S proteasomes and we cannot expect to understand the latter if we do not understand the mechanisms that determine the activity of the former.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge.

claim: The 20S proteasome consists of four stacked seven membered rings (denoted by α7β7β7α7).
source: The 20S proteasome consists of four stacked seven membered rings (denoted by α7β7β7α7).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge.

claim: The proteasome rings form three interconnected cavities, including a pair of antechambers.
source: These rings form three interconnected cavities, including a pair of antechambers through which substrates are passed before reaching the central catalytic chamber.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge.

claim: Antechamber walls interact actively with the substrates by altering their properties and keeping them accessible for hydrolysis.
source: Antechamber walls are not merely structural, but interact actively with the substrates by altering their properties and keeping them accessible for hydrolysis (Ruschak et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Proteasome chambers can store two or more proteins to enable continuous degradation.
source: These proteasome chambers can also store two or more proteins in order to enable continuous degradation (Hutschenreiter et al., 2004; Sharon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The central chamber contains six subunits (two β1, β2 and β5 subunits) that catalyse the peptide-bond hydrolysis.
source: The central chamber contains six subunits (two β1, β2 and β5 subunits) that catalyse the peptide-bond hydrolysis and peptide splicing after binding of the polypeptide substrates nearby their active N-terminal Thr (Vigneron et al., 2004; Borissenko and Groll, 2007; Mishto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established structural and functional knowledge supported by citations.

claim: 20S proteasomes modify their conformations and activity upon peptide-bond hydrolysis.
source: 20S proteasomes modify their conformations and thus in turn their activity upon peptide-bond hydrolysis (Osmulski et al., 2009; Ruschak and Kay, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Binding of regulatory complexes such as 11S or 19S to the proteasome α rings modifies proteasome activity.
source: binding of regulatory complexes such as 11S or 19S to the proteasome α rings (leading to the formation of PA28-capped proteasomes and 26S proteasomes, respectively) (Dick et al., 1996; Emmerich et al., 2000; Köhler et al., 2001; Ruschak and Kay, 2012; Raule et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Non-catalytic modifier sites can activate proteasome activity.
source: activation of non-catalytic modifier sites (Schmidtke et al., 2000; Kisselev et al., 2002, 2003) whose location in the proteasome remain unknown (Liepe et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The location of non-catalytic modifier sites in the proteasome remains unknown.
source: activation of non-catalytic modifier sites (Schmidtke et al., 2000; Kisselev et al., 2002, 2003) whose location in the proteasome remain unknown (Liepe et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Upon an inflammatory stimulus such as IFN-γ the catalytic standard β1, β2 and β5 subunits are replaced by the immuno-subunits β1i, β2i and β5i in newly synthesized immunoproteasome.
source: Upon an inflammatory stimulus such as IFN-γ the catalytic standard β1, β2 and β5 subunits peculiar of the standard proteasome (s-proteasome) are replaced by the immuno-subunits β1i, β2i and β5i in the newly synthesized immunoproteasome (i-proteasome).
evidence: This is established knowledge about proteasome biology.

claim: Proteasome isoforms degrade substrates with different rates, but generate the same peptide pool.
source: Proteasome isoforms degrade substrates with different rates, but generate the same peptide pool (Mishto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The 20S i-proteasome often has a higher polypeptide degradation rate than its standard counterpart.
source: And while there exist differences between substrates, the 20S i-proteasome has been shown often to have a higher polypeptide degradation rate than its standard counterpart (Bellavista et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Different degradation kinetics of specific substrates by s- and i-proteasomes have been suggested to be involved in a variety of pathologies.
source: The question is also of direct medical relevance: different degradation kinetics of specific substrates by s- and i-proteasomes, or i-proteasome carrying genetic polymorphisms/mutations, have been suggested to be involved in a variety of pathologies (Basler et al., 2013; Bellavista et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: i-proteasome deficient mice show altered proteasome-dependent kinetics of pathogen epitope generation.
source: Furthermore, i-proteasome deficient mice show altered proteasome-dependent kinetics of pathogen epitope generation (Basler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Purified mouse 20S proteasomes show substrate inhibition at high substrate concentrations when digesting short fluorogenic peptides in vitro.
source: The in vitro digestion of short fluorogenic peptides by purified mouse 20S proteasomes reveals, however, substrate inhibition at high substrate concentrations (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Proteasome proteolytic activity changes over time as the product accumulates in non-linear fashion.
source: Furthermore, we find that proteasome proteolytic activity, that is, reaction velocity, changes over time as the product accumulates in non-linear fashion (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The reaction velocity for the substrate Suc-LLVY-MCA increases over time.
source: For instance, the reaction velocity for the substrate Suc-LLVY-MCA increases over time (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The temporal profile of proteasome activity is not due to its permanency at 37°C.
source: this temporal profile of proteasome activity is not due to its permanency at 37°C since Suc-LLVY-MCA degradation kinetics of the mouse proteasomes prior storing for 18 hr at 37°C or 4°C do not differ significantly (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Proteasome activity inhibition at high substrate concentrations is observed when using protein homogenate of human T2 cells.
source: Similarly, we detect proteasome activity inhibition at high substrate concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and non-linear accumulation of product over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), when using protein homogenate of human T2 cells, which contains 20S proteasome as well as proteasome regulatory complexes such as 19S and PA28.
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The frequency of peptide-bond hydrolysis after some cleavage sites of polypeptide substrates varies over time.
source: In agreement with the data obtained by using the short fluorogenic substrates, we also observe that the frequency of peptide-bond hydrolysis after some cleavage sites of polypeptide substrates varies over time (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Only a slight reduction in the average length of the peptide products occurs in polypeptide degradations, only at late time points, and only when less than 50% of the substrate is still intact.
source: However, we observe only a slight reduction in the average length of the peptide products in the polypeptide degradations, only at late time points, and only when less than 50% of the substrate is still intact (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Changes in cleavage site usage are already becoming evident at early time points.
source: By contrast, the changes in cleavage site usage are already becoming evident at early time points (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Substrate depletion, product re-entry or further cleavage cannot explain variation in cleavage site usage over time.
source: Therefore substrate depletion, product re-entry or further cleavage cannot explain variation in cleavage site usage over time.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations about timing of changes.

claim: The classical Michaelis-Menten model explains neither the substrate inhibition nor the increasing reaction velocity observed in proteasome kinetics.
source: This scheme is often assumed for enzymatic reactions and forms the basis of the MM model (Figure 2A); but it explains neither the substrate inhibition nor the increasing reaction velocity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by model fitting failures.

claim: The substrate inhibition model fails to reproduce the experimental data for Z-LLE-MCA degradation.
source: However, the substrate inhibition model still fails to reproduce our data, which can be clearly seen in the case of Z-LLE-MCA degradation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B, blue curves).
evidence: This is demonstrated by model fitting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Models with positive feedback on binding or hydrolysis cannot explain substrate inhibition and fail to reproduce experimental data.
source: Even though both mechanisms result in an increased reaction velocity over time, they cannot explain substrate inhibition and fail to reproduce our experimental data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by model fitting failures shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: A transport model based on free diffusion cannot capture the observed data.
source: However, the proteasome gate and the interior surface of the proteasome chambers have strong partial charges, and substrate molecules have been shown to interact at least with the latter, and a transport model based on free diffusion cannot capture the observed data (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by model fitting failure.

claim: The degradation rate of the substrate Bz-VGR-MCA increases in the presence of the peptide LLVY.
source: Indeed, the degradation rate of Suc-LLVY-MCA by mouse proteasome progressively accelerates within 90 min (Figure 1B), and the degradation rate of the substrate Bz-VGR-MCA increases in the presence of the peptide LLVY (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The progressive increase of the enhancing effect of LLVY peptide over time is not due to slow kinetics of the binding to non-catalytic modifier sites.
source: To test whether the progressive increase of the enhancing effect of LLVY peptide over time is due to slow kinetics of the binding to non-catalytic modifier sites we pre-incubate mouse proteasome with LLVY peptide prior to the start of the degradation of the substrates Suc-LLVY-MCA and Bz-VGR-MCA. The enhancing activity of LLVY is maximal for shorter pre-incubation, but the initial acceleration remains the same (Figure 3B). Thus the progressive acceleration over time of the two substrates' degradations is not due to slow binding of the LLVY peptide to non-catalytic modifier sites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pre-incubation experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Peptide-bond hydrolysis is mandatory for the enhancing effect by LLVY peptide.
source: Instead the data suggest that peptide-bond hydrolysis is mandatory for the enhancing effect by LLVY peptide.
evidence: This is inferred from the pre-incubation experimental results.

claim: When mouse 20S proteasome digests Bz-VGR-MCA in presence of Rpt peptides no further enhancement of the degradation rate is seen when the LLVY peptide is added.
source: We can confirm this with the help of Rpt peptides, which are short peptides deriving from subunits of the 19S regulatory complex and known to bind the proteasome α subunit tails and open the gate (Gillette et al., 2008). When mouse 20S proteasome digests the substrates Bz-VGR-MCA in presence of Rpt peptides no further enhancement of the degradation rate is seen when the LLVY peptide is added (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The model with an enhancing regulatory site inside the chambers and an inhibiting regulatory site outside the proteasome best represents the experimental data.
source: The two models with the enhancing regulatory site inside the chambers can reproduce the increased reaction velocity at early time points observed in the data, but only the model with an inhibiting regulatory site is able to fit simultaneously the substrate inhibition and is therefore able to reproduce the time course data in detail (Figure 4B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Bayesian model selection shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The gate-opening regulatory site should be located inside the proteasome chambers.
source: In summary, the integrative analysis suggest that the gate-opening regulatory site proposed previously (Schmidtke et al., 2000; Kisselev et al., 2002) should be located inside the proteasome chambers.
evidence: This is inferred from model selection results and supported by citations.

claim: There is evidence for a transport inhibiting regulatory site located on the proteasome surface.
source: We also find evidence for a transport inhibiting regulatory site located on the proteasome surface.
evidence: This is inferred from model selection results.

claim: The calibrated model reproduces qualitatively the time course of Bz-VGR-MCA and Suc-LLVY-MCA hydrolysis reported by Kisselev et al. (2002).
source: Our calibrated model reproduces qualitatively the time course of Bz-VGR-MCA and Suc-LLVY-MCA hydrolysis of Kisselev et al. (2002) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in silico predictions shown in Figure 4C compared to published data.

claim: The model reproduces dose-response curves for the substrates Suc-LLVY-MCA, Z-LLE-MCA and Bz-VGR-MCA in dependence of the LLVY peptide concentration.
source: In the same study the authors also showed dose-response curves for the substrates Suc-LLVY-MCA and Boc-LRR-MCA in dependence of the LLVY peptide concentration; our model also reproduces the results for the hydrolysis of the substrates Suc-LLVY-MCA, Z-LLE-MCA and Bz-VGR-MCA (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in silico predictions shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The fully parameterised model can explain the altered cleavage site usage over time for polypeptide substrates.
source: As a first step we are interested in whether our fully parameterised model can explain the altered cleavage site usage over time (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is tested by extending the model to polypeptides.

claim: The cleavage site usage variation over time can be explained by transport properties of the substrate and products.
source: This allows us to test whether the cleavage site usage variation over time can be explained by transport properties of the substrate and products.
evidence: This is tested by modeling with substrate-dependent transport parameters.

claim: All possible substrate cleavage site behaviours observed by digesting representative polypeptides can be detected in the modeling framework.
source: In our framework we detect all possible substrate cleavage site behaviours that we observe by digesting representative polypeptides (Figure 1C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in silico simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: Human 20S proteasome purified from T2 and LcL cell lines shows degradation dynamics of short fluorogenic peptide that vary over time.
source: Like we have observed for the mouse proteasome, human 20S proteasome purified from T2 (s-proteasome) and LcL (i-proteasome) cell lines shows degradation dynamics of short fluorogenic peptide that vary over time (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pre-incubation of the proteasome without substrate at 37°C for 18 hr does not alter its activity.
source: This is not due to variation of proteasome functionality as pre-incubation of the proteasome without substrate at 37°C for 18 hr does not alter its activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The substrate cleavage preferences within the LLO291–317 polypeptide by s- and i-proteasomes vary over time.
source: Similarly, the substrate cleavage preferences within the LLO291–317 polypeptide by s- and i-proteasomes vary over time, and not because of product re-entry. We observe modification of the cleavage site usage already at early time points (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Suc-LLVY-MCA is mainly hydrolysed by the β5/β5i subunits.
source: Suc-LLVY-MCA is mainly hydrolysed by the β5/β5i subunits (Mishto et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: i-proteasomes have a higher active site affinity (KaS) with a lower Hill coefficient (na) than s-proteasomes for Suc-LLVY-MCA.
source: and we observe a higher active site affinity (KaS) with a lower Hill coefficient (na) in i- than in s-proteasomes
evidence: This is inferred from posterior parameter distributions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: i-proteasomes have a lower inhibitory site affinity (KiS) with a higher Hill coefficient (ni) compared to s-proteasomes for Suc-LLVY-MCA.
source: similarly i-proteasomes have a lower inhibitory site affinity (KiS) with a higher Hill coefficient (ni) compared to s-proteasomes.
evidence: This is inferred from posterior parameter distributions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The hydrolysis rate (kp) is higher in i-proteasomes than s-proteasomes for Suc-LLVY-MCA.
source: Furthermore, the hydrolysis rate (kp) is higher in i-proteasomes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is inferred from posterior parameter distributions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Z-LLE-MCA is mainly cleaved by β1/β1i active sites.
source: The posterior parameter distribution of Z-LLE-MCA (mainly cleaved by β1/β1i active sites) (Kisselev et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: For Z-LLE-MCA, i-proteasomes have lower affinity to the active site (KaS) and a lower Hill coefficient regarding binding to the inhibitory site (ni) than s-proteasomes.
source: also shows differences in active site parameters, and for i-proteasomes we observe lower affinity to the active site (KaS) and a lower Hill coefficient regarding binding to the inhibitory site (ni).
evidence: This is inferred from posterior parameter distributions.

claim: There is no evidence for differences in parameters related to the active site for Bz-VGR-MCA between s- and i-proteasomes.
source: We find no evidence for differences in parameters related to the active site for Bz-VGR-MCA (mainly cleaved by β2/β2i active sites).
evidence: This is inferred from posterior parameter distributions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Comparing posterior parameter distributions for s- and i-proteasomes reveals differences in parameters related to peptide transport and transport regulation for all three substrates.
source: Comparing posterior parameter distributions for s- and i-proteasomes reveals differences in parameters related to peptide transport and transport regulation for all three substrates (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is inferred from posterior parameter distributions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: All three substrates have altered affinities to the gate between s- and i-proteasomes.
source: All three substrates have altered affinities to the gate (koff/kon: i-proteasome lower than s-proteasome for Suc-LLVY-MCA and Z-LLE-MCA but higher for Bz-VGR-MCA)
evidence: This is inferred from posterior parameter distributions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: All three substrates have altered influx and efflux rates between s- and i-proteasomes.
source: and altered influx and efflux rates (vin, vout: i-proteasome higher for Suc-LLVY-MCA and Bz-VGR-MCA but lower for Z-LLE-MCA).
evidence: This is inferred from posterior parameter distributions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Affinity to the enhancing regulatory site inside the proteasome chambers (Roff/Ron) is higher in i-proteasome for all three substrates.
source: Finally, affinity to the enhancing regulatory site inside the proteasome chambers (Roff/Ron) is higher in i-proteasome for all three substrates.
evidence: This is inferred from posterior parameter distributions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is no evidence for differences in Xenh and τ between s- and i-proteasomes.
source: By contrast, we find no evidence for differences in Xenh and τ.
evidence: This is inferred from posterior parameter distributions.

claim: The marginal posterior parameter distributions for the maximal capacity C do not differ between s- and i-proteasomes.
source: Furthermore, the marginal posterior parameter distributions for the maximal capacity C do not differ between s- and i-proteasomes, which was expected because both isoforms have the same proteasomal cavity volume.
evidence: This is inferred from posterior parameter distributions and expected from structural knowledge.

claim: The presence of the immuno-subunits in the assembled proteasome influences not only active site parameters but also the parameters that regulate substrate transport.
source: In summary, the presence of the immuno-subunits in the assembled proteasome influences not only active site parameters but also the parameters that regulate substrate transport.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analysis of posterior parameter distributions.

claim: For Suc-LLVY-MCA, the initial gate size has the highest impact on product formation.
source: For Suc-LLVY-MCA we find that the initial gate size has the highest impact.
evidence: This is determined by sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The degradation of Z-LLE-MCA is limited by the efficiency of the hydrolysis.
source: The degradation of Z-LLE-MCA is limited by the efficiency of the hydrolysis, which induces the strongest increase in product formation.
evidence: This is determined by sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Peptide transport is the rate limiting step in proteasomal degradation.
source: Overall peptide transport is the rate limiting step in proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is concluded from sensitivity analysis across substrates.

claim: Differences in kinetic parameters between s- and i-proteasomes result in different chamber-filling kinetics.
source: Differences in kinetic parameters between s- and i-proteasomes furthermore result in different chamber-filling kinetics (Figure 6)
evidence: This is demonstrated by in silico simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: The in vitro experiments verify the in silico predictions about the effects of Rpt peptides on substrate hydrolysis by s- and i-proteasomes.
source: The in vitro experiments verify these three nontrivial in silico predictions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of predictions and experimental validation shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Transport is the rate limiting step in proteasomal degradation.
source: But this comparison validates that transport is indeed the rate limiting step (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is validated by experimental confirmation of model predictions.

claim: The 20S proteasome catalyzes the degradation of specific proteins in cells.
source: Modelling helps us to understand how the 20S proteasome catalyzes the degradation of specific proteins in cells (Pickering and Davies, 2012; Ben-Nissan and Sharon, 2014; Höhn and Grune, 2014; Fabre et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In 19S or PA28 single-capped proteasomes all steps considered in the model are still present.
source: Indeed, in 19S or PA28 single-capped proteasomes all steps considered in our model are still present, including the regulation of the gate by non-catalytic modifier site(s) and the gate binding affinity since one of the proteasome gates is not bound to the regulatory complexes and will therefore be regulated as described here.
evidence: This is inferred from structural knowledge about capped proteasomes.

claim: Similar proteasome dynamics over time are observed when using purified 20S proteasome as well as protein homogenates.
source: We observe similar proteasome dynamics over time when using purified 20S proteasome as well as protein homogenates, where 20S proteasomes are surrounded by several regulatory molecules.
evidence: This is observed in experimental data.

claim: The present model describes a core of proteasome features that could reflect proteasome dynamics also in more complex scenarios such as might exist inside the cellular environment.
source: It suggests that with the present model we describe a core of proteasome features that could reflect proteasome dynamics also in more complex scenarios such as might exist inside the cellular environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar dynamics in different experimental setups.

claim: Simple Michaelis-Menten-type models are not capable of describing proteasome dynamics.
source: Simple (e.g., MM-type) models, which have been largely used in analysing proteasome functionality so far, are clearly not capable of describing proteasome dynamics
evidence: This is demonstrated by model comparison and fitting failures.

claim: The cavity of 20S proteasomes is progressively filled by peptides that can further facilitate other molecules to enter the chambers until the effective cavity volume has been almost completely filled.
source: Our analysis suggests that the cavity of 20S proteasomes is progressively filled by peptides that can further facilitate other molecules to enter the chambers until the effective cavity volume has been almost completely filled.
evidence: This is inferred from modeling results.

claim: The estimated numbers of substrate and product molecules (C) that are inside the proteasome cavity are close to the possible maxima.
source: In fact, the estimated numbers of substrate and product molecules (C) that are inside the proteasome cavity are close to the possible maxima (Box 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of model estimates with theoretical calculations in Box 2.

claim: Non-catalytic modifier sites are located inside the proteasome cavity.
source: Peptide accumulation over time leads to activation of non-catalytic modifier sites, which our analysis shows to be located inside the proteasome cavity.
evidence: This is inferred from model selection results.

claim: Substrate transport through the gate and cavities is a key factor in the regulation of the proteolytic process.
source: Substrate transport through the gate and cavities must therefore be a key factor in the regulation of the proteolytic process, despite the fact that it had been largely neglected so far in the quantitative analysis of proteasome dynamics (Liepe et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is concluded from modeling and experimental results, and contrasted with previous work.

claim: Peptide transport is the major rate limiting step in the degradation of short fluorogenic substrates.
source: The integration of data into our mathematical model clearly shows that peptide transport is the major rate limiting step in the degradation of short fluorogenic substrates: all models/hypotheses that do not account for this are soundly rejected.
evidence: This is demonstrated by model selection.

claim: The rate limiting steps for short fluorogenic substrates are conserved across different proteasomes (mouse proteasome and human s- and i-proteasomes).
source: We stress that for the short fluorogenic substrates the rate limiting steps are conserved across the different proteasomes (mouse proteasome and human s- and i-proteasomes).
evidence: This is concluded from comparative analysis.

claim: The interspecies homology of the proteasome structure results in preserving transport characteristics.
source: This in turn suggests that the interspecies homology of the proteasome structure results in preserving transport characteristics, although subtle structural variations can quantitatively modify the transport, as observed by comparing s- and i-proteasomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of rate limiting steps across species and isoforms.

claim: Variation of the transport efficiency typically leads to quantitative changes in the degradation rates of short fluorogenic substrates.
source: Variation of the transport efficiency typically leads to quantitative changes in the degradation rates of short fluorogenic substrates.
evidence: This is concluded from the analysis of transport parameters.

claim: For polypeptides, transport variation could change substrate cleavage-site usage and result in the generation of specific peptide products.
source: For more complex substrates, for example, polypeptides, transport variation could change substrate cleavage-site usage and thus result in the generation of specific peptide products.
evidence: This is inferred from the model extension to polypeptides.

claim: Significant decreases of antigenic peptide amount produced by proteasome could lead to presentation onto MHC class I molecules that is too diminished to trigger CD8+ T cell activation.
source: Indeed, as we have recently shown, significant decreases of antigenic peptide amount produced by proteasome could lead to a presentation onto the MHC class I molecules that is so diminished to be not able to trigger CD8+ T cell activation (Mishto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Modifications of the proteasome gate upon PA28 binding will affect the substrate cleavage-site usage and lead to alterations of MHC class I-restricted epitope repertoire.
source: According to our model, modifications of the proteasome gate upon PA28 binding will for instance affect the substrate cleavage-site usage and lead to the observed alterations of MHC class I-restricted epitope repertoire (Cascio, 2014).
evidence: This is predicted by the model and supported by citation.

claim: Differences in gate and inner channel features are in part responsible for the different degradation rates of short fluorogenic peptides by human s- and i-proteasomes.
source: Differences in gate and inner channel features are in part responsible for the different degradation rates of the short fluorogenic peptides by human s- and i-proteasomes although they diverge also in the activity of the catalytic subunits themselves.
evidence: This is concluded from parameter analysis.

claim: Differences in the gate between s- and i-proteasomes are supported by preferential binding between the α subunits of s- and i-proteasomes and specific regulatory complexes.
source: Differences in the gate between the two proteasome isoforms are supported also by Fabre et al. (2015), who identified preferential binding between the α subunits of s- and i-proteasomes and specific regulatory complexes.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The degradation of the substrate Bz-VGR-MCA is not influenced by differences in the active site-related parameters between s- and i-proteasomes.
source: For instance, the degradation of the substrate Bz-VGR-MCA is not influenced by differences in the active site-related parameters—as is correctly predicted by our model.
evidence: This is predicted by the model and agrees with structural data.

claim: Comparisons of the crystallographic structures of the mouse s- and i-proteasomes identify only minor variations between the β2 and β2i catalytic pockets.
source: This also agrees with comparisons of the crystallographic structures of the mouse s- and i-proteasomes, which identify only minor variations between the β2 and β2i catalytic pockets (Huber et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The catalytic sites of s-proteasome have stronger binding affinity for the substrate Z-LLE-MCA than the i-proteasome.
source: By contrast, the catalytic sites of s-proteasome have stronger binding affinity for the substrate Z-LLE-MCA than the i-proteasome, which could be explained by the structural differences between β1 and β1i catalytic pockets described by Huber et al. (2012).
evidence: This is inferred from parameter analysis and supported by citation.

claim: The i-proteasome has higher substrate-binding affinity, higher hydrolysis rate, and lower cooperativity than the s-proteasome for Suc-LLVY-MCA.
source: For the degradation of the substrate Suc-LLVY-MCA our model predicts that the i-proteasome has higher substrate-binding affinity, higher hydrolysis rate, and lower cooperativity than the s-proteasome.
evidence: This is predicted by the model from parameter analysis.

claim: The β5i pocket is more prone to bind and process substrates than the β5 pocket.
source: This prediction is corroborated by the recent study of Arciniega et al. (2014), who showed that the β5i pocket is more prone to bind and process substrates than the β5 pocket
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Only s-proteasome is able to modify its conformation upon substrate binding to the β5 subunit.
source: however, only s-proteasome is able to modify its conformation upon substrate binding to the β5 subunit (Arciniega et al., 2014), which is also correctly captured by our model as increased cooperativity (ni).
evidence: This is supported by citation and captured by the model.

claim: The i-proteasome has a higher affinity for the enhancing non-catalytic modifier site activated by all three substrates.
source: The outcomes of our integrative analysis suggest that the i-proteasome also has a higher affinity for the enhancing non-catalytic modifier site activated by all three substrates
evidence: This is inferred from parameter analysis.

claim: The enhancer site should be located at the inner surface of the proteasome.
source: given that our model consistently predicts this site to be located at the inner surface, it should now become possible to determine the precise location of the enhancer site using structural techniques.
evidence: This is predicted by the model.
